screens.title: Building and Deploying Your Game
screens.narratorSegment: You’ve reached a milestone: your capstone project is complete and now we convert it into something players can run. Building is the process where Unity compiles scripts, processes assets, and packages everything into a platform-specific output such as a Windows executable or a WebGL folder. In this lesson you will learn the build pipeline, how to set Player Settings that define your game’s identity, how to add the correct scenes to the build, and how to prepare for platform specifics like compression, scripting backends, and mobile signing. We’ll walk through the Build Settings window, the Player Settings inspector, and practical folder and testing strategies so your first build runs reliably. You’ll also encounter common mistakes that break a build and learn quick checks to avoid them. By the end you’ll be able to perform a PC Standalone build and a WebGL build, test them locally, and prepare a simple distribution package for sharing with stakeholders. Think of this step as turning your development sandbox into a finished deliverable that others can install or play. What single setting will you check first when you open your Build Settings?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Building & Deploying
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Building and Deploying Your Game

Compile your Unity project into a platform-ready package. Configure identity, display, scenes, and platform details so players can run your game outside the Editor.

In this lesson
From Build Settings to distribution
Why it matters
A proper build ensures the game runs reliably and appears professional when shared.
Coming up
Player Settings, Scenes in Build, PC and WebGL walkthroughs.
Build Settings
Select platform, manage scenes, and start builds. This is the command center for packaging your game.
Player Settings
Define company, product, icons, version, and resolution behavior that travel with the build.
Distribution
Package executables, WebGL folders, or mobile bundles and test them before sharing.
Explore Key Topics
Scenes In Build
Make sure the correct scenes are added and the first scene is at index 0 so the game starts where you expect.
Platform Options
Scripting backends, compression, and API compatibility differ across PC, WebGL, and mobile; configure per target.
Testing & Distribution
Test built files locally and prepare a zipped package for PC or a WebGL folder for web publishing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical actions you will perform when preparing a build. First, you will understand Unity’s build process: what it does and why settings matter. Knowing this helps you debug build failures and choose suitable options for performance and size. Second, you will configure Player Settings including company and product metadata, icons, splash images, and versioning so your game identifies correctly and looks professional. Third, you will prepare target platforms by selecting the correct platform in Build Settings and adjusting platform-specific options like scripting backend, compression, and A P I levels. Fourth, you will perform a successful build: add scenes, pick an output folder outside Assets, run the build, and verify the executable or WebGL output. Each objective connects a concrete Editor action to a reason: identity, compatibility, performance, or distribution. As you work, use these objectives as verification steps: ask yourself, have I set the product name, added the right scenes, and picked the correct platform options? This habit helps avoid common mistakes and gets your game into players’ hands faster.

screens.title: Practical Skills to Verify
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide breaks the build workflow into verifiable skills you can test as you work. First, add and order scenes in Scenes In Build so the correct starting scene loads. Missing or mis-ordered scenes are a common cause of a blank build. Second, choose output folders outside the Assets directory and create a Builds folder to keep artifacts organized and avoid accidentally committing large binaries. Third, inspect Other Settings for platform-specific parameters such as scripting backend, A P I compatibility level, and compression for WebGL. These settings can change performance and build success. Fourth, apply a testing routine: run the build, verify startup behavior, check icons and splash images, and compare runtime behavior with the Editor. Each item is small but critical; treating them as a checklist reduces failures and saves debugging time. Use these skills as acceptance criteria before you share a build with testers or upload to a web platform. Which verification step will prevent the most frequent build failures in your project?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Verify Skills
Scenes In Build

Ensure the main scene is at index 0 and include all scenes needed at runtime. Forgetting scenes often produces a blank or incomplete build.

Mnemonic
Order matters: start scene first.
Why
Startup scene determines initial player experience and loaded systems.
Folder & Testing Routine

Use a root-level Builds folder outside Assets and name subfolders by platform and version. After building, run the executable or open the WebGL index.html and compare behavior to Editor playback.

Example
Builds/PC/1.0 and Builds/WebGL/1.0
Mistake
Saving builds inside Assets can bloat source control and confuse import steps.

screens.title: What is the Build Process?
screens.narratorSegment: Building is the compilation and packaging step that turns your project from an Editor workspace into files a platform can run. In Unity, the build pipeline compiles managed code, bundles assets, converts shaders and scenes, and produces platform-specific outputs such as a Windows executable with a data folder, or a WebGL folder with an index. html. This matters because some behavior differs outside the Editor: file paths may change, scripting backends behave differently, and certain Editor-only APIs are not available. For example, code that relies on Editor classes will compile in the Editor but fail in a build. A concrete example: if you serialize data to an Editor-only directory or use Editor-specific UI code, the build can throw errors or produce missing content. A common misconception is that Editor play perfectly matches the final build; it often does not because of runtime optimizations, different memory limits, and platform APIs. Key checks during building include ensuring your scenes are added, Player Settings metadata is set, and platform-specific options are chosen. Remember: building is a release step that requires deliberate verification, not just pressing the Build button. What difference would you expect when switching from Mono to IL2CPP on mobile builds?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Building compiles code and packages assets into a platform-specific runnable output; Editor play is not identical to a built runtime.

content.html:
Core Concept

What is the Build Process?

Building compiles scripts and packages assets into an executable or web folder suitable for a chosen target platform.
  • Compiles managed code and bundles assets
  • Processes shaders and platform conversions
  • Creates output specific to the target platform
Key Takeaway

A build is the release representation of your project; always test builds since Editor behavior may differ.

Concrete Example
If you use an Editor-only path or Editor UI class, the build will fail or omit content. Replace Editor-only logic with runtime-safe code guarded by preprocessor directives to avoid errors.
Misconception
Editor play is identical to a built game. It often isn't due to different runtimes and limits.
Pro Tip
Guard platform-specific code with preprocessor directives and test builds early.
Checklist
  1. Add required scenes to Scenes In Build.
  2. Set Player Settings for identity and resolution.
  3. Choose correct scripting backend and compression for platform.

screens.title: Navigate Build Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Start every build by opening File, Build Settings in the Unity Editor. That dialog lists available target platforms such as PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, and iOS. Choose the platform you intend to deliver to and, when needed, click Switch Platform so Unity reimports assets for that target. For a capstone deliverable you will commonly choose PC Standalone for easy sharing or WebGL for browser play. Scenes In Build appears in the same window; drag scenes from the Project window into this list and ensure the first scene is index 0. The Build Settings window also shows development build options and the Build button. A typical workflow: select platform, confirm scenes, open Player Settings to set metadata, then choose a build output folder. Common mistakes here are forgetting to switch platform or failing to include scenes. Switching platform can take time because Unity reimports assets; plan builds around that. As a rule, create a dedicated Builds folder at the project root and name subfolders by platform and version. That keeps output organized and avoids accidental inclusion in source control. Which platform will you target first for sharing your capstone?

keyIdea.title: Build Settings workflow
keyIdea.text: Open Build Settings, select target platform, add scenes, then open Player Settings and choose an output folder before building.

content.html:
Process Flow

Open Build Settings

Navigate to File → Build Settings, pick your target platform, and arrange scenes to include in the final build.
Step 1 — Select Platform
Pick PC Standalone or WebGL. Click Switch Platform when required so Unity reimports assets for that target.
Step 2 — Add Scenes
Drag scenes into Scenes In Build. Make your main scene index 0 so it starts first.
Step 3 — Set Output Folder
Create Builds/PlatformName/Version at the project root and save the build there.
Common Mistakes
  • Not switching platform and suffering incompatible runtime errors.
  • Forgetting to add required scenes, resulting in a blank or wrong startup scene.
  • Saving builds inside Assets which clutters the project and source control.
Pro Tip

Plan platform switches early. Reimporting assets can take several minutes for larger projects.

Example Folder
Builds/PC/1.0 and Builds/WebGL/1.0 keep artifacts separate and versioned.

screens.title: Player Settings: Identity and Branding
screens.narratorSegment: Player Settings define how your built game identifies itself and displays at startup. In Build Settings click Player Settings to open the Inspector where you can set Company Name and Product Name, which appear in metadata and sometimes in save file paths. Set a clear version number such as 1.0 or 1.0.1 so you and players can track releases. Assign a Default Icon to replace the generic desktop icon with something meaningful. For a polished startup, customize a Splash Image or use a custom splash screen to show your logo before the first scene loads. Resolution and Presentation settings live nearby and determine default screen width, fullscreen behavior, and mobile orientation. A practical example: set Company Name to "Cohortia" and Product Name to "[Your Game Title] Capstone" so builds show consistent metadata. A frequent misconception is that missing icons or wrong titles are cosmetic; in practice they affect perceived polish and can confuse testers. Always increment the version when exporting a public build so you can trace feedback to a specific package. After you set these values, they are written into the build and will appear to players.

keyIdea.title: Player metadata
keyIdea.text: Set company and product names, version, icons, and splash screens so the build presents a professional identity and is easier to manage.

content.html:
Definition

Player Settings: Identity and Branding

Set Company Name, Product Name, Version, Default Icon, and Splash Image so players see your branding and metadata is consistent.

Example
Company: Cohortia; Product: [Your Game Title] Capstone; Version: 1.0
Why it matters
Branding and versioning help players and testers identify the build and its release state.
Practical Steps
  1. Open Player Settings from Build Settings.
  2. Set Company Name and Product Name.
  3. Assign a Default Icon and optional Splash Image.
  4. Update Version before building.
Common Mistake

Leaving Company and Product as defaults can show "DefaultCompany" in tabs and metadata, which looks unpolished.

screens.title: Resolution, Presentation, and Platform Options
screens.narratorSegment: Resolution and Presentation in Player Settings control how the game appears when launched. For desktop builds you can set default width and height, whether the game starts fullscreen or windowed, and whether players can resize the window. For WebGL builds the browser imposes additional constraints and you often choose compression formats and memory size under WebGL settings. Other Settings contain platform-specific options: scripting backend choice (Mono or IL2CPP), A P I compatibility level, and platform SDK targets. Choosing IL2CPP tends to produce more optimized binaries and is often recommended for mobile, while Mono gives faster iterative build times. A concrete example: for PC testing set Fullscreen Mode to Windowed so you can quickly switch between Editor and build; for WebGL prefer Brotli compression to reduce upload size. A misconception is to leave defaults; that can cause mismatched resolution or runtime memory shortages on WebGL. When switching platform, review these tabs and adjust settings to the target device constraints. Small adjustments here can fix many platform-specific run-time issues without code changes. Resolution, Presentation, and Platform Options means presentation and platform options determine window behavior, compression, memory, and scripting backend choices that affect performance and compatibility.. In practical terms, how display and backend choices change runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Display & backend
keyIdea.text: Presentation and platform options determine window behavior, compression, memory, and scripting backend choices that affect performance and compatibility.

content.html:
Comparison

Resolution & Presentation

Desktop: control default width, fullscreen mode, and allow resizing. WebGL: use compression and adjust memory size for browser limits.
Desktop Example
Set fullscreen to Windowed for easy testing and allow resolution selection in a settings menu.
WebGL Example
Choose Brotli compression and set an appropriate memory size to avoid out-of-memory errors in the browser.
Scripting Backend

Mono is faster for editor iteration. IL2CPP compiles to native code and often yields better runtime performance, recommended for release builds and many mobile targets.

When to prefer IL2CPP
Performance sensitive releases and mobile store builds.
When to prefer Mono
Faster edit-build cycles during development.
Misconception

Default settings are always safe. They are not; tailor settings to your target to avoid runtime problems.

screens.title: Scenes In Build and Scene Order
screens.narratorSegment: Scenes In Build is the list Unity uses to include scenes in the final package. The scene at index 0 is the first scene Unity loads when the built game starts. To avoid a blank startup, drag your main scene into the list and make sure it sits at index 0. Include all scenes your game loads at runtime; missing scenes lead to runtime errors when code attempts to load an absent scene. A practical workflow is to keep a dedicated main scene that sets up managers and then loads the first gameplay scene, and list both scenes in Scenes In Build. A common mistake is relying on Editor-only scene references or dynamically loading scenes that were never added to the build list. If you need optional scenes for DLC or downloadable content, handle them as separate downloads rather than forgetting to include them. Use scene naming and versioned builds so testers can reproduce issues with the same scene set. Finally, remember to test the built startup sequence: run the executable or WebGL index. html and confirm the initial scene behavior matches the Editor.

keyIdea.title: Scene order
keyIdea.text: Add every runtime scene to Scenes In Build and make the intended startup scene index 0 so the build launches correctly.

content.html:
Process Flow

Scenes In Build

Drag scenes into the list and ensure the startup scene is index 0. Missing scenes cause runtime load errors in builds.

Example Order
0: MainMenuScene, 1: Level1, 2: Level2, 3: Credits
Checklist
Add scenes used by SceneManager.LoadScene and confirm build index matches code expectations.
Misconception

Assuming all scenes referenced in code will be included automatically. They must be listed in Scenes In Build or load will fail in the built game.

Pro Tip

Maintain a build-scene checklist and verify indexes used in code match the list to avoid off-by-one startup errors.

Scenario
If your build starts on an empty screen, check that your intended scene is at index 0 and that all loadable scenes are included.

screens.title: Running a Build: Steps and Folder Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When you click Build in the Build Settings window Unity asks for an output folder and then compiles the project. Create a dedicated Builds folder at the project root and pick a subfolder for the platform and version, for example Builds/PC/1.0. Unity will compile scripts, process assets, and generate the final files—on Windows you will usually get an. exe and a data folder. For WebGL Unity produces an index. html plus supporting data and code folders. After the build completes, test the build immediately by running the executable or opening index. html in a browser, or better, serve the WebGL folder with a local web server to match production behavior. Keep your builds out of the Assets folder to avoid source control bloat. If a build fails, check the Console for compile or asset processing errors. Common culprits include missing references, incompatible plugins, or platform-specific APIs used without guards. A good practice is to tag build folders with the version and date so you can roll back to previous deliverables. What naming scheme will help you track tested builds most reliably?

keyIdea.title: Build execution
keyIdea.text: Choose a clear output folder, run the build, and test the generated files immediately. Organize by platform and version to track releases.

content.html:
Process

Running a Build

Select Build, choose a folder like Builds/PC/1.0, wait for compilation, then test the generated files immediately to confirm behavior.

What is generated
Windows: .exe + Data folder. WebGL: index.html + data/wasm/code resources.
Testing tips
  1. Run the executable and compare to Editor playback.
  2. For WebGL, use a local server to preview the build reliably.
  3. Record issues with the build version and reproduce in Editor if possible.
Common Build Errors
  • Missing references or null objects that only surface at runtime.
  • Plugins or DLLs incompatible with the selected platform.
  • Platform API calls that lack preprocessor guards.
# Example local server command
python -m http.server

# Run this inside your WebGL build folder to preview index.html
Key Takeaway

Always test the built output. Many issues only appear in the built runtime, not in Editor play.

screens.title: Deployment Options: PC, WebGL, Mobile
screens.narratorSegment: Distribution depends on your target. For PC Standalone you typically distribute an executable plus a data folder; the simplest way to share is to zip the entire generated build folder and provide it to players. Make sure you document any external dependencies such as Visual C++ redistributables when required. For WebGL, upload the build folder to a hosting platform or to itch. io to make the game playable in browsers. Remember that some browsers and hosting setups require the correct compression format and sufficient memory allocation. Mobile builds add complexity: Android requires an SDK, package name, and signing key; iOS requires a signing certificate and app store setup. For a capstone, start with PC or WebGL since they are simpler to share with reviewers. A common misconception is that uploading the project folder is the same as a build; it is not. The project folder contains source and assets but not a runnable package. Always deliver the platform-specific build artifacts and include a short README that states the platform, version, and run instructions so testers can reproduce your environment. Deployment Options: PC, WebGL, Mobile means pc builds zip the executable and data, webgl uploads to web hosts, and mobile requires sdks and store signing; choose the simplest route for your audience.. In practical terms, how distribution differs per target and practical sharing methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

PC Standalone
Build produces an executable and data folder. Zip the folder and distribute. Note external dependencies if present.
WebGL
Build creates index.html and data files. Host on a web server or upload to platforms like itch.io to let players run it in a browser.
Mobile
Requires SDKs, signing keys, and store submission workflows. Suitable for later stages; start with PC/WebGL for easy sharing.
Practical Sharing Steps
  1. For PC: zip build folder and attach or upload to cloud storage.
  2. For WebGL: upload folder to a web host or itch.io and confirm index.html runs.
  3. Provide a README with version and run instructions so testers know how to launch the build.

screens.title: Activity: Build for PC and WebGL
screens.narratorSegment: This activity walks you through building your capstone for PC Standalone and WebGL. Open your project and create a simple test scene if needed. First, open File → Build Settings and drag your main scene into Scenes In Build. Make sure it is index 0. Click Player Settings and under Project Settings > Player set Company Name to "Cohortia" and Product Name to "[Your Game Title] Capstone", then set Version to 1.0. For the PC build, select PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, choose Windows as the target, click Build, and when prompted create a folder at Builds/PC and pick it. Wait for the build to finish and then run the produced. exe to test startup and gameplay. For WebGL, open Build Settings again, select WebGL, click Switch Platform and wait for reimport. In WebGL Player Settings, select Brotli compression if available and set an appropriate memory size. Click Build and select Builds/WebGL as the output folder. After completion, open a local server in the WebGL folder using the command python -m http. server and visit the local URL to test. Record any differences and fix issues before sharing. This sequence ensures you practice the exact steps and test both outputs before distribution.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Build Your Capstone for PC and WebGL

  1. Open File → Build Settings. Add your main scene and confirm index 0.
  2. Click Player Settings: set Company Name to Cohortia, Product Name to [Your Game Title] Capstone, Version 1.0, and optionally assign an icon and splash.
  3. PC Build: Select PC, Mac & Linux Standalone → Windows, click Build, choose Builds/PC, wait, then run the .exe to test.
  4. WebGL Build: Select WebGL, click Switch Platform, set compression to Brotli if available, click Build, choose Builds/WebGL, then test using a local server.
  5. Document results and increment the version before the next public build.
Quick Commands
# In your WebGL build folder
python -m http.server

# Then open http://localhost:8000 in your browser
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist and test both builds immediately. Version and folder naming make debugging and sharing much easier.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts are the central anchors for building and deploying a Unity project. First, the Build Process is the compilation and packaging pipeline that creates platform-specific runnable files. Second, Player Settings control game identity and presentation, including company and product names, icons, splash images, and resolution choices that travel with the build. Third, Target Platform decisions determine platform-specific options like scripting backend, compression, and memory; they directly affect performance, compatibility, and build success. Keep these concepts in mind as you follow the practical steps to add scenes, choose an output folder, run builds, and test the final artifacts. They explain why certain checks are necessary and where common mistakes originate. When you prepare a build, ask: did I set Player Settings, include the right scenes, and select the correct platform options? That short checklist will prevent most issues and get your game into players’ hands faster.

screens.narratorSegment: Use this quick reference when preparing a build. First, always check Scenes In Build to confirm the startup scene and any runtime scenes are included. Second, set Player Settings for company and product information, version, icons, and splash screens so the build looks intentional and traces to a release. Third, choose appropriate platform options: scripting backend, compression, and memory settings influence performance and build size. These three reminders will prevent the most frequent build problems: blank startups, incorrect metadata, and platform runtime errors. Before you click Build, run this three-item checklist to avoid lost time and rework. fullNarratorScript:
You’ve reached a milestone: your capstone project is complete and now we convert it into something players can run. Building is the process where Unity compiles scripts, processes assets, and packages everything into a platform-specific output such as a Windows executable or a WebGL folder. In this lesson you will learn the build pipeline, how to set Player Settings that define your game’s identity, how to add the correct scenes to the build, and how to prepare for platform specifics like compression, scripting backends, and mobile signing. We’ll walk through the Build Settings window, the Player Settings inspector, and practical folder and testing strategies so your first build runs reliably. You’ll also encounter common mistakes that break a build and learn quick checks to avoid them. By the end you’ll be able to perform a PC Standalone build and a WebGL build, test them locally, and prepare a simple distribution package for sharing with stakeholders. Think of this step as turning your development sandbox into a finished deliverable that others can install or play. What single setting will you check first when you open your Build Settings?

These learning objectives map to practical actions you will perform when preparing a build. First, you will understand Unity’s build process: what it does and why settings matter. Knowing this helps you debug build failures and choose suitable options for performance and size. Second, you will configure Player Settings including company and product metadata, icons, splash images, and versioning so your game identifies correctly and looks professional. Third, you will prepare target platforms by selecting the correct platform in Build Settings and adjusting platform-specific options like scripting backend, compression, and A P I levels. Fourth, you will perform a successful build: add scenes, pick an output folder outside Assets, run the build, and verify the executable or WebGL output. Each objective connects a concrete Editor action to a reason: identity, compatibility, performance, or distribution. As you work, use these objectives as verification steps: ask yourself, have I set the product name, added the right scenes, and picked the correct platform options? This habit helps avoid common mistakes and gets your game into players’ hands faster.

This second objectives slide breaks the build workflow into verifiable skills you can test as you work. First, add and order scenes in Scenes In Build so the correct starting scene loads. Missing or mis-ordered scenes are a common cause of a blank build. Second, choose output folders outside the Assets directory and create a Builds folder to keep artifacts organized and avoid accidentally committing large binaries. Third, inspect Other Settings for platform-specific parameters such as scripting backend, A P I compatibility level, and compression for WebGL. These settings can change performance and build success. Fourth, apply a testing routine: run the build, verify startup behavior, check icons and splash images, and compare runtime behavior with the Editor. Each item is small but critical; treating them as a checklist reduces failures and saves debugging time. Use these skills as acceptance criteria before you share a build with testers or upload to a web platform. Which verification step will prevent the most frequent build failures in your project?

Building is the compilation and packaging step that turns your project from an Editor workspace into files a platform can run. In Unity, the build pipeline compiles managed code, bundles assets, converts shaders and scenes, and produces platform-specific outputs such as a Windows executable with a data folder, or a WebGL folder with an index. html. This matters because some behavior differs outside the Editor: file paths may change, scripting backends behave differently, and certain Editor-only APIs are not available. For example, code that relies on Editor classes will compile in the Editor but fail in a build. A concrete example: if you serialize data to an Editor-only directory or use Editor-specific UI code, the build can throw errors or produce missing content. A common misconception is that Editor play perfectly matches the final build; it often does not because of runtime optimizations, different memory limits, and platform APIs. Key checks during building include ensuring your scenes are added, Player Settings metadata is set, and platform-specific options are chosen. Remember: building is a release step that requires deliberate verification, not just pressing the Build button. What difference would you expect when switching from Mono to IL2CPP on mobile builds?

Start every build by opening File, Build Settings in the Unity Editor. That dialog lists available target platforms such as PC, Mac & Linux Standalone, WebGL, Android, and iOS. Choose the platform you intend to deliver to and, when needed, click Switch Platform so Unity reimports assets for that target. For a capstone deliverable you will commonly choose PC Standalone for easy sharing or WebGL for browser play. Scenes In Build appears in the same window; drag scenes from the Project window into this list and ensure the first scene is index 0. The Build Settings window also shows development build options and the Build button. A typical workflow: select platform, confirm scenes, open Player Settings to set metadata, then choose a build output folder. Common mistakes here are forgetting to switch platform or failing to include scenes. Switching platform can take time because Unity reimports assets; plan builds around that. As a rule, create a dedicated Builds folder at the project root and name subfolders by platform and version. That keeps output organized and avoids accidental inclusion in source control. Which platform will you target first for sharing your capstone?

Player Settings define how your built game identifies itself and displays at startup. In Build Settings click Player Settings to open the Inspector where you can set Company Name and Product Name, which appear in metadata and sometimes in save file paths. Set a clear version number such as 1.0 or 1.0.1 so you and players can track releases. Assign a Default Icon to replace the generic desktop icon with something meaningful. For a polished startup, customize a Splash Image or use a custom splash screen to show your logo before the first scene loads. Resolution and Presentation settings live nearby and determine default screen width, fullscreen behavior, and mobile orientation. A practical example: set Company Name to "Cohortia" and Product Name to "[Your Game Title] Capstone" so builds show consistent metadata. A frequent misconception is that missing icons or wrong titles are cosmetic; in practice they affect perceived polish and can confuse testers. Always increment the version when exporting a public build so you can trace feedback to a specific package. After you set these values, they are written into the build and will appear to players.

Resolution and Presentation in Player Settings control how the game appears when launched. For desktop builds you can set default width and height, whether the game starts fullscreen or windowed, and whether players can resize the window. For WebGL builds the browser imposes additional constraints and you often choose compression formats and memory size under WebGL settings. Other Settings contain platform-specific options: scripting backend choice (Mono or IL2CPP), A P I compatibility level, and platform SDK targets. Choosing IL2CPP tends to produce more optimized binaries and is often recommended for mobile, while Mono gives faster iterative build times. A concrete example: for PC testing set Fullscreen Mode to Windowed so you can quickly switch between Editor and build; for WebGL prefer Brotli compression to reduce upload size. A misconception is to leave defaults; that can cause mismatched resolution or runtime memory shortages on WebGL. When switching platform, review these tabs and adjust settings to the target device constraints. Small adjustments here can fix many platform-specific run-time issues without code changes. Resolution, Presentation, and Platform Options means presentation and platform options determine window behavior, compression, memory, and scripting backend choices that affect performance and compatibility.. In practical terms, how display and backend choices change runtime behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scenes In Build is the list Unity uses to include scenes in the final package. The scene at index 0 is the first scene Unity loads when the built game starts. To avoid a blank startup, drag your main scene into the list and make sure it sits at index 0. Include all scenes your game loads at runtime; missing scenes lead to runtime errors when code attempts to load an absent scene. A practical workflow is to keep a dedicated main scene that sets up managers and then loads the first gameplay scene, and list both scenes in Scenes In Build. A common mistake is relying on Editor-only scene references or dynamically loading scenes that were never added to the build list. If you need optional scenes for DLC or downloadable content, handle them as separate downloads rather than forgetting to include them. Use scene naming and versioned builds so testers can reproduce issues with the same scene set. Finally, remember to test the built startup sequence: run the executable or WebGL index. html and confirm the initial scene behavior matches the Editor.

When you click Build in the Build Settings window Unity asks for an output folder and then compiles the project. Create a dedicated Builds folder at the project root and pick a subfolder for the platform and version, for example Builds/PC/1.0. Unity will compile scripts, process assets, and generate the final files—on Windows you will usually get an. exe and a data folder. For WebGL Unity produces an index. html plus supporting data and code folders. After the build completes, test the build immediately by running the executable or opening index. html in a browser, or better, serve the WebGL folder with a local web server to match production behavior. Keep your builds out of the Assets folder to avoid source control bloat. If a build fails, check the Console for compile or asset processing errors. Common culprits include missing references, incompatible plugins, or platform-specific APIs used without guards. A good practice is to tag build folders with the version and date so you can roll back to previous deliverables. What naming scheme will help you track tested builds most reliably?

Distribution depends on your target. For PC Standalone you typically distribute an executable plus a data folder; the simplest way to share is to zip the entire generated build folder and provide it to players. Make sure you document any external dependencies such as Visual C++ redistributables when required. For WebGL, upload the build folder to a hosting platform or to itch. io to make the game playable in browsers. Remember that some browsers and hosting setups require the correct compression format and sufficient memory allocation. Mobile builds add complexity: Android requires an SDK, package name, and signing key; iOS requires a signing certificate and app store setup. For a capstone, start with PC or WebGL since they are simpler to share with reviewers. A common misconception is that uploading the project folder is the same as a build; it is not. The project folder contains source and assets but not a runnable package. Always deliver the platform-specific build artifacts and include a short README that states the platform, version, and run instructions so testers can reproduce your environment. Deployment Options: PC, WebGL, Mobile means pc builds zip the executable and data, webgl uploads to web hosts, and mobile requires sdks and store signing; choose the simplest route for your audience.. In practical terms, how distribution differs per target and practical sharing methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
